title: Biomedical-specific extraction candidate assessment (entity extraction only)
method: Lightweight option assessed first per the closure directive: a pure dictionary/alias matcher built directly from nlu/normalization.py's existing curated tables (DISEASE_TABLE, GENE_TABLE, COMPOUND_TABLE - 24 real entities, live-API-verified), doing longest-match substring scanning with word-boundary checks, zero LLM calls.
why_this_result_is_NOT_evidence_the_dict: nlu_benchmark_v1.1.0's 105 template-generated examples (A-G) were built by parameterizing over the SAME 24-entity curated list that DISEASE_TABLE/GENE_TABLE/COMPOUND_TABLE contain (see the benchmark's own 'provenance' field). A dictionary matcher built from that same table is therefore GUARANTEED perfect recall on this benchmark by construction - this is circular, not a genuine generalization test.

In production, any query naming a disease/gene/compound NOT in the 24-entry table would get zero recall from a pure dictionary matcher (it can only find exact known strings), whereas Candidates A and B use an LLM with broad biomedical world knowledge and correctly extract entities never seen during normalization-table construction.

The benchmark cannot currently be used to fairly compare generalization because it has no gold examples built from OUT-OF-TABLE entities (a known limitation already flagged in evaluation/v2/nlu_benchmark_v1.json's known_limitations - 'normalization accuracy does not generalize to entities outside that table' - the same caveat applies to a dictionary-only extractor's RECALL, not just normalization accuracy).
heavier_option_considered: scispaCy or a comparable biomedical NER model - NOT installed or evaluated this pass. Given the dictionary-matcher result above already shows that the *ceiling* of a pure-lookup approach is unmeasurable on this benchmark (perfect by construction) and that a real dependency add (scispaCy: large model downloads, spaCy pipeline dependency, license review, Apple-Silicon-wheel verification) is a nontrivial cost, and given Candidate B's LLM-based extraction already achieves 0.767-0.745 F1 with a credible root cause for the gap (recall-driven, not a labeling/vocabulary problem - see PHASE2_REOPEN_ANALYSIS.md), adding scispaCy was judged NOT justified without first re-measuring Candidate B post the B_VS_G_RULE / canonicalization fixes in this closure round. Left as an open item if Candidate B's post-fix entity F1 (artifacts/v2/nlu_closure_entitytype_b_dev.json) still fails the item 18 entity-regression gate.
conclusion: No new dependency added. The existing curated normalization tables already provide the equivalent value a lightweight dictionary matcher would add, as part of nlu/normalization.py's deterministic normalization layer downstream of LLM-proposed spans (which is the correct place for a lookup table - confirming/canonicalizing an LLM's proposed entity, not replacing entity DETECTION, which requires generalizing beyond a fixed vocabulary). A standalone dictionary-only entity extractor is not recommended as a production replacement or supplement for Candidate B's LLM-based extraction: it would silently fail (zero recall, not an explicit abstention) on any entity outside the current 24-term table, which is worse than an LLM's imperfect-but-generalizing recall for a research-assistant product.
decision: Keep current architecture (LLM extraction + deterministic normalization lookup). Do not add scispaCy or expand the dictionary matcher into a standalone extraction candidate this closure pass.
